Practical Pandas, Matplotlib and Seaborn Training¶

Data Cleaning, Data Manipulation and Data Visualization - A Complete Hands-On Course¶

Prepared by: Kajola Gbenga Data Scientist & AI Engineer

About this notebook¶

This notebook is a complete, line-by-line practical course built around one deliberately messy retail sales dataset (retail_sales_raw.csv, also available as retail_sales_training.xlsx). Every technique is demonstrated on real data with real problems, not on a toy example, so that each idea can be taught, explained and reproduced in a classroom.

The notebook is organised into four parts:

  1. Loading and first exploration of the raw data.
  2. Data cleaning - every common pandas cleaning operation, explained line by line.
  3. Data manipulation - selecting, sorting, grouping, reshaping, merging, time series and more.
  4. Data visualization - every major chart type in Matplotlib and every major chart type in Seaborn, each with an explanation of when and why you would use it.

Read the markdown cell above each code cell first - it explains, line by line, what the code below it does and why. Then run the code cell and study the output.

0. Setup - importing the libraries we need¶

Line by line:

  • import pandas as pd loads the pandas library, the core tool for tabular data in Python, and gives it the short alias pd.
  • import numpy as np loads NumPy, which pandas is built on top of, and which we use directly for numeric operations such as np.where and np.select.
  • import matplotlib.pyplot as plt loads Matplotlib's plotting interface, aliased as plt.
  • import seaborn as sns loads Seaborn, a statistical plotting library built on top of Matplotlib, aliased as sns.
  • %matplotlib inline is a notebook "magic command" that tells Jupyter to render charts directly inside the notebook.
  • pd.set_option(...) widens how many columns and rows pandas prints, so wide tables are not truncated while we teach.
  • sns.set_theme(...) sets a consistent, readable visual style for every chart in the notebook.
  • warnings.filterwarnings('ignore') silences noisy, non-critical warnings so the teaching output stays clean.
In [1]:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.ticker as mticker
import seaborn as sns
import warnings

warnings.filterwarnings('ignore')

%matplotlib inline

pd.set_option('display.max_columns', 60)
pd.set_option('display.width', 160)
pd.set_option('display.max_rows', 100)

sns.set_theme(style='whitegrid', palette='deep')
plt.rcParams['figure.figsize'] = (10, 6)
plt.rcParams['axes.titlesize'] = 14
plt.rcParams['axes.titleweight'] = 'bold'

  • df.dtypes shows the data type pandas inferred for every column - this is the single most important first check in any cleaning project, because a column that should be numeric but was inferred as object (text) tells you immediately that it contains dirty values.

1.5 Summary information: info() and describe()¶

Line by line:

  • df.info() prints the row count, column count, non-null count per column, and dtype per column in one compact report - the fastest way to see where missing data lives.
  • df.describe() gives summary statistics (count, mean, std, min, quartiles, max) for numeric columns only, by default.
  • df.describe(include='object') gives the equivalent summary (count, unique, top, freq) for text columns.
  • df.describe(include='all') combines both, with NaN shown where a statistic does not apply.

1.6 Counting missing values and duplicates¶

Line by line:

  • df.isna() returns a same-shaped DataFrame of True/False values, True where data is missing.
  • .sum() on that adds the True values down each column, giving a missing-value count per column.
  • df.isna().sum().sum() gives the grand total of missing cells in the whole table.
  • df.duplicated() flags rows that are an exact repeat of an earlier row.
  • df.duplicated().sum() counts how many exact duplicate rows exist.

1.7 Unique values and value counts¶

Line by line:

  • df['Country'].unique() lists every distinct value that appears in the Country column - this is how we discover that "Nigeria", "nigeria", "NIGERIA" and " Nigeria" are all being treated as different categories.
  • df['Country'].nunique() counts how many distinct values there are.
  • df['OrderStatus'].value_counts() counts how often each distinct value occurs, sorted from most to least common - the classic first step for spotting inconsistent categorical data.
  • value_counts(dropna=False) includes missing values in the count.

PART 2 - Data Cleaning¶

This is the heart of the course. We will work through every major category of data cleaning in pandas, in the order a real project usually needs them:

2.1 Handling missing values 2.2 Removing duplicate rows 2.3 Fixing data types (numbers stored as text, dates stored as text) 2.4 Cleaning text columns (case, whitespace, inconsistent spelling) 2.5 Standardising categorical values with mapping dictionaries 2.6 Detecting and handling outliers and impossible values 2.7 Renaming and reordering columns 2.8 Final validation of the cleaned dataset

We will build a new, cleaned DataFrame called clean step by step, so df always stays available as the original untouched raw data for comparison.

2.1 Handling missing values¶

Line by line:

  • df.dropna() removes any row that has at least one missing value anywhere - useful only when missingness is rare and rows are cheap to lose. We do not use this on the whole table here, because it would throw away most of our rows.
  • df.dropna(subset=['OrderID']) removes rows only where the named column(s) are missing - this is safe to use on OrderID because a row with no order id is not usable at all.
  • df.dropna(how='all') removes a row only if every column in it is missing - this is exactly the right tool for removing the fully blank rows we saw in the data.
  • df.fillna(value) fills missing values with a fixed value.
  • df['Rating'].fillna(df['Rating'].median()) fills missing numeric values with the column median - a common, robust choice because the median is not distorted by outliers.
  • df['CustomerGender'].fillna('Unknown') fills a missing category with an explicit "Unknown" label, which is usually better than deleting the row or guessing.
  • df.fillna(method='ffill') (forward fill) copies the last valid value forward - most useful in time-ordered data.
  • df.interpolate() fills numeric gaps by estimating a value between the surrounding numbers.
In [16]:
clean = df.copy()

# Step 1: drop rows that are completely blank (every column missing)
before = len(clean)
clean = clean.dropna(how='all')
print(f'Removed {before - len(clean)} fully blank rows. Remaining rows: {len(clean)}')

# Step 2: an OrderID is mandatory - a row without one cannot be reconciled with any sale
before = len(clean)
clean = clean.dropna(subset=['OrderID'])
print(f'Removed {before - len(clean)} rows with a missing OrderID. Remaining rows: {len(clean)}')

Removed 0 fully blank rows. Remaining rows: 1539
Removed 4 rows with a missing OrderID. Remaining rows: 1535

# (c) forward fill and interpolate, shown on a small numeric example so the mechanics are visible
example = pd.Series([10, np.nan, np.nan, 40, np.nan, 60])
print('Original:      ', example.tolist())
print('Forward fill:  ', example.ffill().tolist())

print('Interpolated:  ', example.interpolate().tolist())

2.2 Removing duplicate rows¶

Line by line:

  • clean.duplicated() flags exact duplicate rows (every column identical).
  • clean.drop_duplicates() removes exact duplicate rows, keeping the first occurrence by default.
  • clean.drop_duplicates(subset=['OrderID'], keep='first') removes rows that share the same OrderID, even if other columns differ slightly (our "near duplicate, re-keyed" rows) - this is the more realistic real-world rule, because the business key is the order id, not the whole row.
  • keep='last' keeps the most recent duplicate instead of the first; keep=False drops every copy of a duplicated row, keeping none of them.
In [20]:
print('Exact duplicate rows before removal:', clean.duplicated().sum())
clean = clean.drop_duplicates()
print('Exact duplicate rows after removal:', clean.duplicated().sum())

print()
print('Rows sharing an OrderID before removal:', clean.duplicated(subset=['OrderID']).sum())
clean = clean.drop_duplicates(subset=['OrderID'], keep='first')
print('Rows remaining:', len(clean))

Exact duplicate rows before removal: 0
Exact duplicate rows after removal: 0

Rows remaining: 1500

2.3 Fixing data types¶

Several columns look numeric or date-like but were loaded as plain text (object), because a few dirty values in each column stopped pandas from inferring the correct type automatically.

Line by line:

  • clean['UnitPrice'].str.replace('$', '', regex=False) removes the currency symbol.
  • .str.replace(',', '', regex=False) removes thousands separators.
  • pd.to_numeric(series, errors='coerce') converts text to numbers, turning anything that still cannot be parsed (like the "N/A" values) into NaN instead of raising an error - this is the safest way to convert a dirty numeric column.
  • pd.to_datetime(series, errors='coerce', dayfirst=False) parses many different date string formats into real datetime64 values in one call; unparseable strings become NaT (Not a Time), the datetime equivalent of NaN.
  • clean['Quantity'].astype('Int64') casts to pandas' nullable integer type (capital I), which, unlike NumPy's int64, is allowed to hold missing values.
In [21]:
# Clean the price column: strip currency symbols and commas, then convert to numeric
clean['UnitPrice'] = (
    clean['UnitPrice']
    .astype(str)
    .str.replace('$', '', regex=False)
    .str.replace(',', '', regex=False)
    .str.strip()
)
clean['UnitPrice'] = pd.to_numeric(clean['UnitPrice'], errors='coerce')
print(clean['UnitPrice'].describe())

# Parse the OrderDate column, which mixes five different date string formats, into real dates

2.4 Cleaning text columns¶

Line by line:

  • .str.strip() removes leading and trailing whitespace (" Nigeria" and "Nigeria " both become "Nigeria").
  • .str.lower() / .str.upper() / .str.title() normalise letter case.
  • .str.replace(pattern, repl, regex=True) performs a find-and-replace, optionally using a regular expression.
  • .str.contains('pattern') returns True/False for whether each value contains a substring or pattern - useful for flagging malformed values, such as the malformed emails in this data.
  • .str.extract(r'(pattern)') pulls a substring out of each value using a regex capture group.
  • .str.split(',').str[0] splits a string on a separator and keeps one piece - used below to fix names stored as "Lastname, Firstname".
In [24]:
# Standardise CustomerName: strip whitespace, fix 'Lastname, Firstname' pattern, then Title Case
def normalise_name(name):
    if pd.isna(name):
        return name
    name = str(name).strip()
    if ',' in name:
        last, first = [p.strip() for p in name.split(',', 1)]
        name = f'{first} {last}'
    return name.title()

clean['CustomerName'] = clean['CustomerName'].apply(normalise_name)

# Flag malformed emails using str.contains with a simple regex, before deciding how to handle them
valid_email_pattern = r'^[\w\.-]+@[\w\.-]+\.\w+$'
is_valid_email = clean['CustomerEmail'].str.contains(valid_email_pattern, regex=True, na=False)
print('Valid-looking emails:', is_valid_email.sum())
print('Missing or malformed emails:', (~is_valid_email).sum())

# Malformed (non-null but not matching the pattern) emails are set to missing, to be handled like any other NaN
clean.loc[(~is_valid_email) & clean['CustomerEmail'].notna(), 'CustomerEmail'] = np.nan

2.5 Standardising categorical values with a mapping dictionary¶

Title-casing fixed some inconsistency, but country names need a proper lookup dictionary, because "USA", "U.S.A" and "US" do not share a common pattern that .str.title() can fix.

Line by line:

  • We first strip and title-case the raw values to shrink the number of distinct spellings.
  • country_map is a Python dictionary from every messy variant we still see to one clean, canonical name.
  • clean['Country'].map(country_map) looks each value up in the dictionary and returns the clean version; any value not found in the dictionary becomes NaN (a useful side effect that doubles as a validation check).
  • np.where(condition, value_if_true, value_if_false) is shown as an alternative for a simple two-way recoding.
In [27]:
clean['Country'] = clean['Country'].astype(str).str.strip().str.title()
clean.loc[clean['Country'] == 'Nan', 'Country'] = np.nan

print('Distinct values before dictionary mapping:')
print(sorted(clean['Country'].dropna().unique()))

# np.where as a quick alternative for simple two-way recoding, demonstrated on CustomerGender
clean['CustomerGender'] = clean['CustomerGender'].astype(str).str.strip().str.upper().str[0]
clean.loc[~clean['CustomerGender'].isin(['M', 'F']), 'CustomerGender'] = np.nan
clean['CustomerGender'] = np.where(clean['CustomerGender'] == 'M', 'Male',
                            np.where(clean['CustomerGender'] == 'F', 'Female', 'Unknown'))
clean.loc[clean['CustomerGender'] == 'Unknown', 'CustomerGender'] = np.nan
clean['CustomerGender'].value_counts(dropna=False)

2.6 Detecting and handling outliers and impossible values¶

Line by line:

  • The IQR (interquartile range) method: compute the 25th percentile (Q1) and 75th percentile (Q3), then flag anything below Q1 - 1.5*IQR or above Q3 + 1.5*IQR as a statistical outlier.
  • The domain-knowledge method: some values are impossible regardless of statistics - a negative age, an age above roughly 110, a discount above 1 (100 percent), or a rating outside 1 to 5. These are cleaned using direct boolean conditions, not statistics.
  • .clip(lower, upper) caps values at a floor and/or ceiling instead of removing them.
In [30]:
# Domain-knowledge cleaning: values that are impossible no matter their statistical distribution
before_invalid_age = ((clean['CustomerAge'] < 0) | (clean['CustomerAge'] > 110)).sum()
clean.loc[(clean['CustomerAge'] < 0) | (clean['CustomerAge'] > 110), 'CustomerAge'] = pd.NA
print('Impossible ages set to missing:', before_invalid_age)

before_invalid_qty = ((clean['Quantity'] <= 0)).sum()
clean.loc[clean['Quantity'] <= 0, 'Quantity'] = pd.NA
print('Zero or negative quantities set to missing:', before_invalid_qty)

before_invalid_discount = (clean['Discount'] > 1).sum()
clean.loc[clean['Discount'] > 1, 'Discount'] = np.nan
print('Discounts above 100 percent set to missing:', before_invalid_discount)

before_invalid_rating = (~clean['Rating'].between(1, 5) & clean['Rating'].notna()).sum()
clean.loc[~clean['Rating'].between(1, 5), 'Rating'] = pd.NA
print('Ratings outside 1 to 5 set to missing:', before_invalid_rating)

Impossible ages set to missing: 42
Zero or negative quantities set to missing: 47
Discounts above 100 percent set to missing: 15
Ratings outside 1 to 5 set to missing: 12
In [31]:
# Statistical outlier detection with the IQR method, applied to UnitPrice
Q1 = clean['UnitPrice'].quantile(0.25)
Q3 = clean['UnitPrice'].quantile(0.75)
IQR = Q3 - Q1
lower_bound = Q1 - 1.5 * IQR
upper_bound = Q3 + 1.5 * IQR

outliers = clean[(clean['UnitPrice'] < lower_bound) | (clean['UnitPrice'] > upper_bound)]
print(f'IQR bounds: [{lower_bound:.2f}, {upper_bound:.2f}]')
print(f'Number of statistical price outliers: {len(outliers)}')

# Rather than deleting them (they are legitimate premium electronics, not errors), we cap (clip) them
clean['UnitPrice'] = clean['UnitPrice'].clip(lower=0, upper=upper_bound)

2.7 Renaming and reordering columns¶

Line by line:

  • clean.rename(columns={...}) renames specific columns using a dictionary of old name to new name.
  • clean.columns = [...] replaces every column name at once - fast, but you must supply a full list in the correct order.
  • clean[new_order] reindexes the columns into a chosen order by passing a list of column names.
In [32]:
clean = clean.rename(columns={
    'CustomerAge': 'Age',
    'CustomerGender': 'Gender',
    'CustomerEmail': 'Email',
    'CustomerName': 'Name',
})

new_order = ['OrderID', 'OrderDate', 'Name', 'Email', 'Gender', 'Age', 'Country',
             'ProductCategory', 'ProductName', 'Quantity', 'UnitPrice', 'Discount',
             'ShippingCost', 'PaymentMethod', 'OrderStatus', 'Rating', 'SalesRep', 'Notes']
clean = clean[new_order]

2.8 Adding a derived column and final validation of the cleaned dataset¶

Line by line:

  • We create NetSales, a new numeric column computed from other columns - Quantity * UnitPrice * (1 - Discount). Rows where Discount is missing use .fillna(0) first, since no discount recorded most often means no discount was applied.
  • clean.isna().sum() gives a final missing-value report on the cleaned data, for comparison with Part 1.
  • clean.duplicated().sum() confirms no duplicate rows remain.
  • clean.reset_index(drop=True) rebuilds the row index as a clean 0..n-1 sequence after all the dropping and filtering above (row numbers were left with gaps).
In [33]:
clean['NetSales'] = (
    clean['Quantity'].astype('Float64')
    * clean['UnitPrice']
    * (1 - clean['Discount'].fillna(0))
)

clean = clean.reset_index(drop=True)

print('Final cleaned shape:', clean.shape)
print()
print('Missing values remaining per column:')
print(clean.isna().sum())
print()
print('Duplicate rows remaining:', clean.duplicated().sum())

PART 3 - Data Manipulation¶

With a clean dataset in hand, this part covers the pandas operations used every day to answer business questions: selecting and filtering, sorting, creating columns, grouping and aggregating, pivoting and reshaping, merging with other tables, binning, ranking, time series operations and multi-index operations.

We load the lookup tables we will need for merging in this part as well.

3.1 Selecting and filtering¶

Line by line:

  • clean['Country'] selects a single column as a Series.
  • clean[['Country', 'NetSales']] selects several columns as a DataFrame (note the double brackets).
  • clean.loc[row_condition, column_list] selects by label - rows matching a boolean condition, and specific columns.
  • clean.iloc[0:5, 0:3] selects by position - the first 5 rows and first 3 columns, regardless of labels.
  • Boolean indexing: clean[clean['Country'] == 'Nigeria'] keeps only rows where the condition is True.
  • .isin([...]) keeps rows whose value is in a given list.
  • .between(a, b) keeps rows whose numeric value falls in a range (inclusive by default).
  • .query('expression') filters using a readable string expression, useful for combining several conditions.

nigeria_sales = clean.loc[clean['Country'] == 'Nigeria', ['OrderID', 'ProductName', 'NetSales']]

3.2 Sorting¶

Line by line:

  • clean.sort_values('NetSales', ascending=False) sorts rows by one column, largest first.
  • clean.sort_values(['Country', 'NetSales'], ascending=[True, False]) sorts by several columns at once, with an independent direction for each.
  • clean.nlargest(5, 'NetSales') is a fast shortcut for "top 5 rows by this column", equivalent to sorting and taking the head, but clearer to read.
  • clean.nsmallest(5, 'NetSales') is the same idea for the smallest values.

3.3 Creating new columns¶

Line by line:

  • Direct arithmetic on columns (vectorised) is always the fastest way to create a new column, as shown already with NetSales.
  • .apply(function, axis=1) runs a Python function once per row, useful when the logic is too complex for simple arithmetic; slower than vectorised code, so used only when needed.
  • lambda is a small, unnamed inline function, often paired with .apply() or .map().
  • np.select(conditions, choices, default) evaluates several conditions in order and assigns the matching choice - the vectorised, fast equivalent of a chain of if/elif/else.
In [43]:
clean['OrderYear'] = clean['OrderDate'].dt.year
clean['OrderMonth'] = clean['OrderDate'].dt.month_name()
clean['OrderWeekday'] = clean['OrderDate'].dt.day_name()

# np.select: assign an age band using several ordered conditions at once (vectorised, fast)
age_float = clean['Age'].astype('Float64')
conditions = [
    (age_float < 25).fillna(False),
    (age_float.between(25, 34)).fillna(False),
    (age_float.between(35, 49)).fillna(False),
    (age_float >= 50).fillna(False),
]

clean['AgeBand'] = np.select(conditions, choices, default='Unknown')

3.4 GroupBy and aggregation¶

Line by line:

  • clean.groupby('ProductCategory')['NetSales'].sum() splits the data into groups by category, then sums NetSales within each group - the classic split-apply-combine pattern.
  • .groupby([...]) can group by more than one column at once, producing a hierarchical result.
  • .agg({...}) applies a different aggregation to each column in the same call.
  • Named aggregation (pd.NamedAgg) lets you compute several statistics on the same column and give each resulting column a clear, chosen name, avoiding awkward multi-level column headers.
  • .reset_index() turns the grouped index back into ordinary columns, which is usually easier to read and to plot.

3.5 Pivot tables and cross tabulation¶

Line by line:

  • pd.pivot_table(data, values, index, columns, aggfunc) reshapes long data into a wide summary grid - rows become index, one distinct value per columns becomes its own column, and cells hold the aggregated values.
  • pd.crosstab(row_series, col_series) is a specialised pivot table that simply counts how often each combination of two categorical variables occurs - the fastest way to build a frequency table between two categories.
  • margins=True adds row and column totals to either function.
In [49]:
pivot_sales = pd.pivot_table(
    clean, values='NetSales', index='ProductCategory', columns='OrderYear',
    aggfunc='sum', fill_value=0, margins=True, margins_name='Total'
)

3.6 Reshaping data: melt, pivot, stack and unstack¶

Line by line:

  • pd.melt(wide_df, id_vars=[...], value_vars=[...]) converts wide data (one column per category) into long / tidy data (one row per category), the format most plotting and modelling functions expect.
  • .pivot(index=, columns=, values=) is the inverse of melt - it turns long data back into wide data (it does not aggregate; the index/columns combination must already be unique).
  • .stack() moves the innermost column level into the row index, making the table taller and narrower.
  • .unstack() is the inverse - it moves a row index level out into columns, making the table wider.
In [51]:
wide = pivot_sales.drop(columns='Total').drop(index='Total').reset_index()
wide.columns = wide.columns.astype(str)

3.7 Merging, joining and concatenating¶

Line by line:

  • pd.merge(left, right, on='key', how='left') combines two tables on a shared key column, the same idea as a SQL join. how controls which rows survive:
    • 'inner' keeps only keys present in both tables.
    • 'left' keeps every row of the left table, filling with NaN where the right table has no match.
    • 'right' keeps every row of the right table.
    • 'outer' keeps every key from either table.
  • left.join(right) is a convenience method for merging on the index instead of a column.
  • pd.concat([df1, df2]) stacks tables - axis=0 (default) stacks rows on top of each other; axis=1 places tables side by side, aligning on the index.
In [55]:
merged = clean.merge(country_region, on='Country', how='left')
merged = merged.merge(category_target, on='ProductCategory', how='left')
merged = merged.merge(sales_rep_lookup, on='SalesRep', how='left')

print(merged.shape)
merged[['OrderID', 'Country', 'Region', 'CurrencyCode', 'ProductCategory',
        'CategoryManager', 'SalesRep', 'Team']].head()

# inner vs left vs outer, demonstrated on two small example tables

right_tbl = pd.DataFrame({'key': ['B', 'C', 'D'], 'right_val': [20, 30, 40]})

print()

3.8 Binning numeric data with cut and qcut¶

Line by line:

  • pd.cut(series, bins=[...], labels=[...]) groups numeric values into bins with boundaries you choose - equal-width or custom-width ranges.
  • pd.qcut(series, q=4, labels=[...]) groups numeric values into bins that each contain roughly the same number of rows (quantiles) - useful for building balanced segments such as spending quartiles.
In [58]:
clean['SalesBand'] = pd.cut(
    clean['NetSales'], bins=[0, 100, 300, 700, np.inf],
    labels=['Small (0-100)', 'Medium (100-300)', 'Large (300-700)', 'Very Large (700+)']
)
clean['SalesBand'].value_counts().sort_index()

                                  labels=['Q1 - Lowest', 'Q2', 'Q3', 'Q4 - Highest'])

3.9 Ranking and cumulative statistics¶

Line by line:

  • .rank(ascending=False) assigns a rank to each value, largest = rank 1.
  • .cumsum() running total; .cumprod() running product; .cummax() / .cummin() running max / min.
  • .diff() difference from the previous row; .pct_change() percentage change from the previous row - both are especially useful once data is sorted by date, for measuring period-over-period change.
In [60]:
category_rank = clean.groupby('ProductCategory')['NetSales'].sum().rank(ascending=False)
category_rank.sort_values()

Groceries          6.0
Name: NetSales, dtype: Float64
In [61]:
monthly = clean.dropna(subset=['OrderDate']).set_index('OrderDate').sort_index()['NetSales'].resample('MS').sum()
monthly_df = monthly.to_frame('MonthlySales')
monthly_df['CumulativeSales'] = monthly_df['MonthlySales'].cumsum()
monthly_df['MonthOverMonthChangePct'] = monthly_df['MonthlySales'].pct_change() * 100

3.10 Time series operations¶

Line by line:

  • .dt.year, .dt.month, .dt.day_name(), .dt.quarter (the .dt accessor) pull date parts out of a datetime column.
  • .set_index('OrderDate') makes the date column the row index, which is required for time-series-specific tools such as resampling.
  • .resample('MS').sum() groups a datetime-indexed series into calendar buckets ('MS' = month start, 'W' = week, 'Q' = quarter, 'Y' = year) and aggregates each bucket - conceptually a groupby specialised for time.
  • .rolling(window=3).mean() computes a moving average over a trailing window of periods, smoothing out short-term noise to reveal the underlying trend.
In [62]:
ts = clean.dropna(subset=['OrderDate']).set_index('OrderDate').sort_index()

daily_sales = ts['NetSales'].resample('D').sum()
monthly_sales = ts['NetSales'].resample('MS').sum()
quarterly_sales = ts['NetSales'].resample('QE').sum()

print('Daily series length:', len(daily_sales))
print('Monthly series length:', len(monthly_sales))
print('Quarterly series length:', len(quarterly_sales))

monthly_sales.head()

3.11 MultiIndex (hierarchical index) basics¶

Line by line:

  • Grouping by more than one column produces a MultiIndex - an index with more than one level.
  • .loc['Nigeria'] on a MultiIndex selects every row belonging to that outer level.
  • .loc[('Nigeria', 'Electronics')] selects one specific combination of outer and inner level.
  • .swaplevel() exchanges which level is outer and which is inner.
In [64]:
multi = clean.groupby(['Country', 'ProductCategory'])['NetSales'].sum()
print(multi.index[:5])
print()
print(multi.loc['Nigeria'])

3.12 Applying functions: apply, map and applymap¶

Line by line:

  • Series.map(dict_or_function) transforms every value in a single column, one value at a time - we already used this for Country.
  • DataFrame.apply(function, axis=1) runs a function once per row (or axis=0, once per column).
  • DataFrame.map(function) (formerly applymap) runs a function on every individual cell in a DataFrame - shown below formatting every numeric column for display.
  • Vectorised operations are preferred over apply whenever possible - they run in optimised C code rather than a slow Python loop over rows. apply is a fallback for logic that truly cannot be expressed with vectorised pandas or NumPy operations.
In [66]:
numeric_preview = clean[['UnitPrice', 'NetSales']].head()
formatted = numeric_preview.map(lambda x: f'{x:,.2f}' if pd.notna(x) else x)
formatted

3.13 Exporting the manipulated dataset¶

Line by line:

  • merged.to_csv(path, index=False) writes the enriched table (after merging in the lookup tables) back out to CSV, without writing the row index as a column.
  • monthly_sales.to_frame().to_excel(path) writes a time series summary out to Excel for sharing with non-technical stakeholders.
In [67]:
merged.to_csv('retail_sales_merged.csv', index=False)
monthly_sales.to_frame('MonthlySales').to_excel('monthly_sales_summary.xlsx')
print('Exports complete: retail_sales_merged.csv, monthly_sales_summary.xlsx')

Exports complete: retail_sales_merged.csv, monthly_sales_summary.xlsx

PART 4 - Data Visualization with Matplotlib¶

Matplotlib is the foundational plotting library in Python - Seaborn (Part 5) is built on top of it. This part works through every major Matplotlib chart type, using the cleaned and merged retail sales data. Each chart is shown with the full code needed to build it, labelled and titled the way a chart intended for a report or a dashboard should be.

We first prepare a few small, reusable summary tables that most of the charts below will plot.

In [68]:
plot_df = merged.dropna(subset=['NetSales', 'OrderDate']).copy()

# Convert pandas nullable dtypes (Int64 / Float64) to plain NumPy dtypes for chart compatibility
for col in ['Age', 'Quantity', 'Rating']:
    plot_df[col] = plot_df[col].astype('float64')
plot_df['NetSales'] = plot_df['NetSales'].astype('float64')

cat_sales = plot_df.groupby('ProductCategory')['NetSales'].sum().sort_values(ascending=False)
monthly_sales_plot = plot_df.set_index('OrderDate').sort_index()['NetSales'].resample('MS').sum()
region_sales = plot_df.groupby('Region')['NetSales'].sum().sort_values(ascending=False)
status_counts = plot_df['OrderStatus'].value_counts()
country_year = plot_df.groupby(['Country', 'OrderYear'])['NetSales'].sum().unstack(fill_value=0)

cat_sales
Out[68]:

Furniture          524889.133063

Fashion            156851.093000

4.1 Line chart¶

Line by line:

  • fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(...)) creates a figure (the whole canvas) and an axes object (the individual chart) - the recommended, explicit way to build a Matplotlib chart.
  • ax.plot(x, y, marker='o', ...) draws a line connecting the data points, with a circular marker at each point.
  • ax.set_title / set_xlabel / set_ylabel label the chart.
  • ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter and plt.xticks(rotation=...) keep date labels readable.
  • fig.tight_layout() removes wasted whitespace so labels are not cut off.
In [69]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 5))
ax.plot(monthly_sales_plot.index, monthly_sales_plot.values, marker='o', color='#1F4E78', linewidth=2)
ax.set_title('Monthly Net Sales Over Time (Matplotlib Line Chart)')
ax.set_xlabel('Month')
ax.set_ylabel('Net Sales (USD)')
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(mticker.FuncFormatter(lambda x, _: f'{x:,.0f}'))
plt.xticks(rotation=45)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

4.2 Vertical bar chart¶

Line by line:

  • ax.bar(categories, values, color=...) draws one vertical bar per category.
  • ax.bar_label(bars, fmt=...) writes the value on top of each bar automatically.
In [70]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
bars = ax.bar(cat_sales.index, cat_sales.values, color='#2E86AB')
ax.set_title('Total Net Sales by Product Category (Matplotlib Bar Chart)')
ax.set_xlabel('Product Category')
ax.set_ylabel('Net Sales (USD)')
ax.bar_label(bars, fmt='{:,.0f}', padding=3)
plt.xticks(rotation=20)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

4.3 Horizontal bar chart¶

Line by line:

  • ax.barh(categories, values) draws horizontal bars - often more readable than vertical bars when category labels are long, since the text reads left to right naturally.
In [71]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))
ax.barh(region_sales.index, region_sales.values, color='#A23B72')
ax.set_title('Total Net Sales by Region (Matplotlib Horizontal Bar Chart)')
ax.set_xlabel('Net Sales (USD)')
ax.invert_yaxis()
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

4.4 Stacked bar chart¶

Line by line:

  • Plotting a second ax.bar(..., bottom=first_values) on top of the first stacks the two series, since bottom tells Matplotlib where the new bars should start rather than starting them at zero.
In [72]:
years = country_year.columns.tolist()
top_countries = plot_df.groupby('Country')['NetSales'].sum().nlargest(5).index
stack_data = country_year.loc[top_countries]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
bottom = np.zeros(len(stack_data))
colors = plt.cm.viridis(np.linspace(0.15, 0.85, len(years)))
for year, color in zip(years, colors):
    ax.bar(stack_data.index, stack_data[year], bottom=bottom, label=str(year), color=color)
    bottom += stack_data[year].values

ax.set_title('Net Sales by Country, Stacked by Year (Matplotlib Stacked Bar Chart)')
ax.set_ylabel('Net Sales (USD)')
ax.legend(title='Year')
plt.xticks(rotation=20)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

4.5 Grouped (clustered) bar chart¶

Line by line:

  • To place bars for different years side by side rather than stacked, we offset each year's bar positions by a small amount using np.arange and a width calculated from the number of groups.
In [73]:
x = np.arange(len(stack_data))
width = 0.8 / len(years)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 6))
for i, (year, color) in enumerate(zip(years, colors)):
    ax.bar(x + i * width, stack_data[year], width=width, label=str(year), color=color)

ax.set_title('Net Sales by Country and Year (Matplotlib Grouped Bar Chart)')
ax.set_xticks(x + width * (len(years) - 1) / 2)
ax.set_xticklabels(stack_data.index, rotation=20)
ax.set_ylabel('Net Sales (USD)')
ax.legend(title='Year')
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

4.6 Histogram¶

Line by line:

  • ax.hist(values, bins=30) splits the numeric range into 30 equal-width bins and counts how many observations fall in each - the standard chart for seeing the shape of a distribution.
In [74]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
ax.hist(plot_df['UnitPrice'].dropna(), bins=30, color='#F18F01', edgecolor='white')
ax.set_title('Distribution of Unit Price (Matplotlib Histogram)')
ax.set_xlabel('Unit Price (USD)')
ax.set_ylabel('Frequency')
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

4.7 Box plot¶

Line by line:

  • ax.boxplot([...], labels=[...]) draws one box-and-whisker summary (median, quartiles, whiskers, outlier points) per group passed in - a compact way to compare spread and outliers across categories.
In [75]:
box_data = [plot_df.loc[plot_df['ProductCategory'] == cat, 'NetSales'].dropna()
            for cat in cat_sales.index]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
ax.boxplot(box_data, labels=cat_sales.index, showmeans=True)
ax.set_title('Net Sales Spread by Product Category (Matplotlib Box Plot)')
ax.set_ylabel('Net Sales (USD)')
plt.xticks(rotation=20)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

4.8 Scatter plot (and bubble chart)¶

Line by line:

  • ax.scatter(x, y) plots one point per row, for seeing the relationship between two numeric variables.
  • Passing s= (size) mapped from a third numeric variable and c= (colour) mapped from a fourth turns the same chart into a bubble chart, encoding up to four variables in one plot.
In [76]:
sample = plot_df.dropna(subset=['UnitPrice', 'NetSales', 'Quantity', 'Rating']).sample(
    n=min(300, len(plot_df)), random_state=1)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
scatter = ax.scatter(sample['UnitPrice'], sample['NetSales'],
                      s=sample['Quantity'].astype(float) * 15,
                      c=sample['Rating'].astype(float), cmap='viridis', alpha=0.7, edgecolor='white')
ax.set_title('Unit Price vs Net Sales, Sized by Quantity, Coloured by Rating (Matplotlib Bubble Chart)')
ax.set_xlabel('Unit Price (USD)')
ax.set_ylabel('Net Sales (USD)')
cbar = fig.colorbar(scatter, ax=ax)
cbar.set_label('Rating')
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

4.9 Pie chart¶

Line by line:

  • ax.pie(values, labels=..., autopct=...) draws a pie chart; autopct formats the percentage label shown inside each slice. Pie charts read best with five or fewer slices, so we group smaller categories together first where necessary.
In [77]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 8))
ax.pie(status_counts.values, labels=status_counts.index, autopct='%1.1f%%',
       startangle=90, colors=plt.cm.Set2.colors, wedgeprops={'edgecolor': 'white'})
ax.set_title('Share of Orders by Order Status (Matplotlib Pie Chart)')
ax.axis('equal')
plt.show()

4.10 Area chart and stacked area chart¶

Line by line:

  • ax.fill_between(x, y) shades the area under a line - a single-series area chart.
  • ax.stackplot(x, y1, y2, ..., labels=[...]) draws several series stacked on top of one another, useful for showing how a total is composed of parts over time.
In [78]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 5))
ax.fill_between(monthly_sales_plot.index, monthly_sales_plot.values, color='#2E86AB', alpha=0.4)
ax.plot(monthly_sales_plot.index, monthly_sales_plot.values, color='#2E86AB', linewidth=2)
ax.set_title('Monthly Net Sales (Matplotlib Area Chart)')
ax.set_ylabel('Net Sales (USD)')
plt.xticks(rotation=45)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
In [79]:
monthly_by_cat = plot_df.set_index('OrderDate').groupby('ProductCategory')['NetSales'].resample('QE').sum().unstack(0).fillna(0)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 6))
ax.stackplot(monthly_by_cat.index, [monthly_by_cat[c] for c in monthly_by_cat.columns],
             labels=monthly_by_cat.columns, alpha=0.85)
ax.set_title('Quarterly Net Sales by Category (Matplotlib Stacked Area Chart)')
ax.set_ylabel('Net Sales (USD)')
ax.legend(loc='upper left', fontsize=8)
plt.xticks(rotation=45)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

4.11 Step plot¶

Line by line:

  • ax.step(x, y, where='mid') draws a stair-step line instead of a smooth diagonal line between points - appropriate when a value is constant between observations, such as a monthly target that only changes once a month.
In [80]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 5))
ax.step(monthly_sales_plot.index, monthly_sales_plot.values, where='mid', color='#C73E1D', linewidth=2)
ax.set_title('Monthly Net Sales (Matplotlib Step Plot)')
ax.set_ylabel('Net Sales (USD)')
plt.xticks(rotation=45)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

4.12 Stem plot¶

Line by line:

  • ax.stem(x, y) draws a vertical line (stem) from zero up to each data point with a marker at the top - useful for emphasising discrete, individual values rather than a continuous trend.
In [81]:
last_12 = monthly_sales_plot.tail(12)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 5))
ax.stem(range(len(last_12)), last_12.values)
ax.set_xticks(range(len(last_12)))
ax.set_xticklabels([d.strftime('%b %Y') for d in last_12.index], rotation=45)
ax.set_title('Net Sales for the Last 12 Months (Matplotlib Stem Plot)')
ax.set_ylabel('Net Sales (USD)')
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

4.13 Error bar plot¶

Line by line:

  • ax.errorbar(x, y, yerr=...) plots a point for each category with a vertical bar showing uncertainty (here, the standard deviation of net sales within each category) - communicating not just the average but how much it varies.
In [82]:
cat_stats = plot_df.groupby('ProductCategory')['NetSales'].agg(['mean', 'std']).sort_values('mean', ascending=False)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
ax.errorbar(cat_stats.index, cat_stats['mean'], yerr=cat_stats['std'], fmt='o', capsize=6,
            color='#1F4E78', ecolor='#A23B72', markersize=8)
ax.set_title('Average Net Sales by Category with Standard Deviation (Matplotlib Error Bar Plot)')
ax.set_ylabel('Net Sales (USD)')
plt.xticks(rotation=20)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

4.14 Dual axis (twin axes) chart¶

Line by line:

  • ax2 = ax1.twinx() creates a second y-axis that shares the same x-axis as the first - used when plotting two series with very different scales (here, sales in dollars against an order count).
In [83]:
monthly_orders = plot_df.set_index('OrderDate').sort_index()['OrderID'].resample('MS').count()

fig, ax1 = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 6))
ax1.plot(monthly_sales_plot.index, monthly_sales_plot.values, color='#1F4E78', marker='o', label='Net Sales')
ax1.set_xlabel('Month')
ax1.set_ylabel('Net Sales (USD)', color='#1F4E78')
ax1.tick_params(axis='y', labelcolor='#1F4E78')

ax2 = ax1.twinx()
ax2.plot(monthly_orders.index, monthly_orders.values, color='#C73E1D', marker='s', label='Order Count')
ax2.set_ylabel('Number of Orders', color='#C73E1D')
ax2.tick_params(axis='y', labelcolor='#C73E1D')

ax1.set_title('Monthly Net Sales and Order Count (Matplotlib Dual Axis Chart)')
plt.xticks(rotation=45)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

4.15 Subplots (multi-panel figure)¶

Line by line:

  • plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, figsize=...) returns a grid of axes objects at once, letting several related charts share one figure - the basis of a simple dashboard.
In [84]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(13, 10))

axes[0, 0].bar(cat_sales.index, cat_sales.values, color='#2E86AB')
axes[0, 0].set_title('Net Sales by Category')
axes[0, 0].tick_params(axis='x', rotation=30)

axes[0, 1].hist(plot_df['UnitPrice'].dropna(), bins=25, color='#F18F01')
axes[0, 1].set_title('Unit Price Distribution')

axes[1, 0].plot(monthly_sales_plot.index, monthly_sales_plot.values, color='#1F4E78', marker='o')
axes[1, 0].set_title('Monthly Net Sales Trend')
axes[1, 0].tick_params(axis='x', rotation=45)

axes[1, 1].pie(status_counts.values, labels=status_counts.index, autopct='%1.0f%%', colors=plt.cm.Set2.colors)
axes[1, 1].set_title('Order Status Share')

fig.suptitle('Retail Sales - Executive Summary (Matplotlib Subplots)', fontsize=16, fontweight='bold')
fig.tight_layout(rect=[0, 0, 1, 0.96])
plt.show()

4.16 Saving a chart to a file¶

Line by line:

  • fig.savefig(path, dpi=200, bbox_inches='tight') exports the current figure to an image file at high resolution, trimming excess whitespace - the standard way to produce a chart for a slide deck or a Word document (used later to build the training manual).
In [85]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
bars = ax.bar(cat_sales.index, cat_sales.values, color='#2E86AB')
ax.set_title('Total Net Sales by Product Category')
ax.bar_label(bars, fmt='{:,.0f}')
plt.xticks(rotation=20)
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig('chart_category_sales.png', dpi=200, bbox_inches='tight')
plt.show()
print('Chart saved to chart_category_sales.png')

Chart saved to chart_category_sales.png

PART 5 - Data Visualization with Seaborn¶

Seaborn is built on top of Matplotlib and is specialised for statistical graphics: it works directly with tidy (long-format) DataFrames and columns of category labels, and it computes many statistics (means, confidence intervals, regression lines, densities) automatically.

This part works through every major Seaborn chart type on the same cleaned data.

5.1 Scatter plot¶

Line by line:

  • sns.scatterplot(data=df, x=, y=, hue=, size=) plots one point per row directly from a DataFrame; hue colours points by a category, size scales points by a numeric column - both handled automatically, including drawing the legend.
In [86]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
sns.scatterplot(data=sample, x='UnitPrice', y='NetSales', hue='ProductCategory', size='Quantity',
                 sizes=(20, 200), alpha=0.75, ax=ax)
ax.set_title('Unit Price vs Net Sales by Category (Seaborn Scatter Plot)')
ax.legend(bbox_to_anchor=(1.02, 1), loc='upper left', fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

5.2 Line plot¶

Line by line:

  • sns.lineplot(data=df, x=, y=, hue=) draws a line per group and, when there are multiple observations per x value, automatically shades a confidence interval band around the line.
In [87]:
monthly_cat = plot_df.set_index('OrderDate').groupby('ProductCategory')['NetSales'].resample('MS').sum().reset_index()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 6))
sns.lineplot(data=monthly_cat, x='OrderDate', y='NetSales', hue='ProductCategory', marker='o', ax=ax)
ax.set_title('Monthly Net Sales by Category (Seaborn Line Plot)')
ax.legend(bbox_to_anchor=(1.02, 1), loc='upper left', fontsize=8)
plt.xticks(rotation=45)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

5.3 Bar plot¶

Line by line:

  • sns.barplot(data=df, x=, y=, estimator=, errorbar=) groups the data by x and plots the aggregated value (mean, by default) as a bar, with an error bar showing uncertainty around that estimate - Seaborn does the grouping and aggregating internally, unlike Matplotlib's bar.
In [88]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
sns.barplot(data=plot_df, x='ProductCategory', y='NetSales', estimator='mean', errorbar='sd',
            hue='ProductCategory', legend=False, palette='crest', ax=ax)
ax.set_title('Average Net Sales by Category, with Standard Deviation (Seaborn Bar Plot)')
plt.xticks(rotation=20)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

5.4 Count plot¶

Line by line:

  • sns.countplot(data=df, x=) counts how many rows fall into each category and plots the counts as bars - the Seaborn equivalent of value_counts().plot(kind='bar'), with cleaner defaults.
In [89]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 6))
sns.countplot(data=plot_df, x='OrderStatus', order=plot_df['OrderStatus'].value_counts().index,
              hue='OrderStatus', legend=False, palette='flare', ax=ax)
ax.set_title('Number of Orders by Status (Seaborn Count Plot)')
plt.xticks(rotation=20)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

5.5 Box plot¶

Line by line:

  • sns.boxplot(data=df, x=, y=, hue=) draws the same box-and-whisker summaries as Matplotlib's boxplot, but reads directly from a tidy DataFrame and can split each box further by a hue category.
In [90]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 6))
sns.boxplot(data=plot_df, x='ProductCategory', y='NetSales', hue='Gender', palette='Set2', ax=ax)
ax.set_title('Net Sales Spread by Category and Gender (Seaborn Box Plot)')
plt.xticks(rotation=20)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

5.6 Violin plot¶

Line by line:

  • sns.violinplot(...) combines a box plot with a rotated, mirrored density plot on each side, showing the full shape of the distribution (where values cluster) as well as the summary statistics a box plot shows.
In [91]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 6))
sns.violinplot(data=plot_df, x='ProductCategory', y='NetSales', hue='ProductCategory',
               legend=False, palette='mako', ax=ax)
ax.set_title('Net Sales Distribution Shape by Category (Seaborn Violin Plot)')
plt.xticks(rotation=20)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

5.7 Strip plot¶

Line by line:

  • sns.stripplot(...) plots every individual observation as a small, slightly jittered dot along a categorical axis - useful for seeing the raw data points and the sample size behind a summary chart.
In [92]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 6))
sns.stripplot(data=sample, x='ProductCategory', y='NetSales', hue='ProductCategory',
              legend=False, alpha=0.6, palette='deep', ax=ax)
ax.set_title('Individual Sales Observations by Category (Seaborn Strip Plot)')
plt.xticks(rotation=20)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

5.8 Swarm plot¶

Line by line:

  • sns.swarmplot(...) is like a strip plot, but it arranges points so they never overlap, giving a clearer picture of density at each value - best used on a modestly sized sample, as shown here.
In [93]:
small_sample = plot_df.dropna(subset=['NetSales']).sample(n=min(150, len(plot_df)), random_state=2)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 6))
sns.swarmplot(data=small_sample, x='ProductCategory', y='NetSales', hue='ProductCategory',
              legend=False, size=4, palette='viridis', ax=ax)
ax.set_title('Sales Observations by Category, Non-Overlapping (Seaborn Swarm Plot)')
plt.xticks(rotation=20)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

5.9 Histogram (histplot) with KDE¶

Line by line:

  • sns.histplot(data=df, x=, kde=True, hue=) draws a histogram and can overlay a smoothed kernel density estimate (KDE) line on top, and can split the histogram by a category automatically.
In [94]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
sns.histplot(data=plot_df, x='UnitPrice', kde=True, bins=30, color='#2E86AB', ax=ax)
ax.set_title('Distribution of Unit Price with Density Curve (Seaborn Histogram)')
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

5.10 KDE plot¶

Line by line:

  • sns.kdeplot(data=df, x=, hue=, fill=True) plots only the smoothed density curve (no bars), making it easy to compare the shape of several distributions overlaid on one chart.
In [95]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
sns.kdeplot(data=plot_df, x='NetSales', hue='ProductCategory', fill=True, alpha=0.25,
            common_norm=False, ax=ax)
ax.set_title('Net Sales Density by Category (Seaborn KDE Plot)')
ax.set_xlim(0, plot_df['NetSales'].quantile(0.98))
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

5.11 ECDF plot¶

Line by line:

  • sns.ecdfplot(data=df, x=) plots the empirical cumulative distribution function - for any point on the x-axis, the curve shows what proportion of observations are at or below it, a precise alternative to reading percentiles off a histogram.
In [96]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
sns.ecdfplot(data=plot_df, x='NetSales', hue='ProductCategory', ax=ax)
ax.set_title('Cumulative Distribution of Net Sales by Category (Seaborn ECDF Plot)')
ax.set_xlim(0, plot_df['NetSales'].quantile(0.98))
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

5.12 Heatmap (correlation matrix)¶

Line by line:

  • df[cols].corr() computes the pairwise Pearson correlation between numeric columns.
  • sns.heatmap(matrix, annot=True, cmap=...) colours each cell by its value and writes the numeric value inside the cell - the standard way to visualise a correlation matrix at a glance.
In [97]:
numeric_cols = ['Age', 'Quantity', 'UnitPrice', 'Discount', 'ShippingCost', 'Rating', 'NetSales']
corr_matrix = plot_df[numeric_cols].astype(float).corr()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 7))
sns.heatmap(corr_matrix, annot=True, fmt='.2f', cmap='coolwarm', center=0, square=True, ax=ax)
ax.set_title('Correlation Matrix of Numeric Variables (Seaborn Heatmap)')
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

5.13 Heatmap (pivot table of category by month)¶

Line by line:

  • The same sns.heatmap function is equally useful on any numeric grid, not only correlation matrices - here it visualises a category-by-month sales pivot table, making seasonal patterns visible by colour.
In [98]:
heat_pivot = pd.pivot_table(plot_df, values='NetSales', index='ProductCategory', columns='OrderMonth', aggfunc='sum', fill_value=0)
month_order = ['January','February','March','April','May','June','July','August','September','October','November','December']
heat_pivot = heat_pivot.reindex(columns=[m for m in month_order if m in heat_pivot.columns])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(13, 6))
sns.heatmap(heat_pivot, cmap='YlGnBu', linewidths=0.5, ax=ax)
ax.set_title('Net Sales by Category and Month (Seaborn Heatmap)')
plt.xticks(rotation=45)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

5.14 Regression plot (regplot / lmplot)¶

Line by line:

  • sns.regplot(data=df, x=, y=) draws a scatter plot with a fitted linear regression line and its confidence interval overlaid - useful for a quick visual read of whether two numeric variables are related.
  • sns.lmplot(...) does the same, but as a figure-level function that can automatically split the regression into small multiples by a category using col= or row=.
In [99]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
sns.regplot(data=sample, x='UnitPrice', y='NetSales', scatter_kws={'alpha': 0.4}, line_kws={'color': 'red'}, ax=ax)
ax.set_title('Unit Price vs Net Sales with Fitted Trend Line (Seaborn Regression Plot)')
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
In [100]:
g = sns.lmplot(data=sample, x='UnitPrice', y='NetSales', col='Gender', height=5, aspect=1,
                scatter_kws={'alpha': 0.4})
g.figure.suptitle('Unit Price vs Net Sales by Gender (Seaborn lmplot, Small Multiples)', y=1.05)
plt.show()

5.15 Pair plot¶

Line by line:

  • sns.pairplot(data=df, vars=[...], hue=) builds a full grid of scatter plots for every pair of chosen numeric variables, with histograms (or KDEs) on the diagonal - a fast way to scan several relationships and distributions at once, split by a category colour.
In [101]:
pair_sample = plot_df.dropna(subset=['UnitPrice', 'NetSales', 'Age', 'Rating']).sample(
    n=min(250, len(plot_df)), random_state=3)

g = sns.pairplot(pair_sample, vars=['UnitPrice', 'NetSales', 'Age'], hue='ProductCategory',
                  diag_kind='kde', plot_kws={'alpha': 0.5, 's': 25}, height=2.6)
g.figure.suptitle('Pairwise Relationships Between Key Numeric Variables (Seaborn Pair Plot)', y=1.02)
plt.show()

5.16 Joint plot¶

Line by line:

  • sns.jointplot(data=df, x=, y=, kind=) combines a central scatter (or hex-bin, or KDE) plot with the marginal distribution of each variable shown along the top and right edges - kind can be 'scatter', 'hex', 'kde', 'reg', among others.
In [102]:
g = sns.jointplot(data=sample, x='UnitPrice', y='NetSales', kind='hex', height=7, cmap='mako')
g.figure.suptitle('Unit Price vs Net Sales with Marginal Distributions (Seaborn Joint Plot)', y=1.02)
plt.show()

5.17 Cat plot (figure-level categorical plotting)¶

Line by line:

  • sns.catplot(data=df, x=, y=, kind=, col=) is a figure-level function that can produce any of Seaborn's categorical plot types ('bar', 'box', 'violin', 'strip', 'swarm', 'point') and automatically split them into a grid of small multiples using col= or row=.
In [103]:
g = sns.catplot(data=plot_df, x='OrderStatus', y='NetSales', kind='box', col='Region',
                 col_wrap=3, height=3.5, aspect=1.1, palette='Set3',
                 order=plot_df['OrderStatus'].value_counts().index)
g.figure.suptitle('Net Sales by Order Status, Split by Region (Seaborn Cat Plot)', y=1.02)
g.set_xticklabels(rotation=30)
plt.show()

5.18 Point plot¶

Line by line:

  • sns.pointplot(data=df, x=, y=, hue=) plots the mean of y for each category as a point, connected by a line, with an error bar - useful for comparing trends across an ordered category, such as spotting which day of the week performs best.
In [104]:
weekday_order = ['Monday','Tuesday','Wednesday','Thursday','Friday','Saturday','Sunday']
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
sns.pointplot(data=plot_df, x='OrderWeekday', y='NetSales', order=weekday_order,
              errorbar='sd', color='#1F4E78', ax=ax)
ax.set_title('Average Net Sales by Day of the Week (Seaborn Point Plot)')
plt.xticks(rotation=20)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

5.19 Facet grid¶

Line by line:

  • sns.FacetGrid(data, col=, row=) builds an empty grid of small charts split by one or two categorical variables.
  • .map_dataframe(plotting_function, x=, y=) draws the same chart type into every cell of the grid.
  • .add_legend() adds one shared legend for the whole grid.
In [105]:
g = sns.FacetGrid(plot_df, col='ProductCategory', col_wrap=3, height=3.2, aspect=1.2)
g.map_dataframe(sns.histplot, x='NetSales', bins=20, color='#2E86AB')
g.set_titles(col_template='{col_name}')
g.figure.suptitle('Net Sales Distribution by Category (Seaborn Facet Grid)', y=1.03)
plt.show()

5.20 Styling: themes, palettes and context¶

Line by line:

  • sns.set_theme(style=, palette=) (used at the very top of the notebook) sets the default look for every chart drawn afterwards - style controls the background grid ('whitegrid', 'darkgrid', 'white', 'dark', 'ticks'), palette controls the default colour sequence.
  • sns.set_context('talk') scales up font sizes and line widths for presentation use, versus 'paper' for compact, print-ready figures.
  • These calls affect every subsequent chart, so they are normally set once, near the top of a notebook or script - demonstrated here on one chart, then reset back to the notebook default.
In [106]:
with sns.axes_style('darkgrid'), sns.plotting_context('talk'):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
    sns.barplot(data=plot_df, x='ProductCategory', y='NetSales', estimator='sum',
                hue='ProductCategory', legend=False, palette='rocket', ax=ax)
    ax.set_title('Total Net Sales by Category (Dark Grid Style, Talk Context)')
    plt.xticks(rotation=20)
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

sns.set_theme(style='whitegrid', palette='deep')  # restore the notebook default

PART 6 - Bringing It Together: A Mini Dashboard¶

A short closing example that combines several of the techniques from this notebook - grouping, pivoting, and a multi-panel Matplotlib and Seaborn figure - into one summary view, the kind of output a training session usually ends on.

In [107]:
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(15, 10))
gs = fig.add_gridspec(2, 2)

ax1 = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 0])
ax1.plot(monthly_sales_plot.index, monthly_sales_plot.values, color='#1F4E78', marker='o')
ax1.set_title('Monthly Net Sales Trend')
ax1.tick_params(axis='x', rotation=45)

ax2 = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 1])
sns.barplot(data=plot_df, x='ProductCategory', y='NetSales', estimator='sum',
            hue='ProductCategory', legend=False, palette='crest', ax=ax2)
ax2.set_title('Total Net Sales by Category')
ax2.tick_params(axis='x', rotation=20)

ax3 = fig.add_subplot(gs[1, 0])
sns.boxplot(data=plot_df, x='Region', y='NetSales', hue='Region', legend=False, palette='Set2', ax=ax3)
ax3.set_title('Net Sales Spread by Region')
ax3.tick_params(axis='x', rotation=20)

ax4 = fig.add_subplot(gs[1, 1])
sns.heatmap(corr_matrix, annot=True, fmt='.2f', cmap='coolwarm', center=0, ax=ax4, cbar=False)
ax4.set_title('Correlation Between Numeric Variables')

fig.suptitle('Retail Sales Training Dataset - Summary Dashboard', fontsize=17, fontweight='bold')
fig.tight_layout(rect=[0, 0, 1, 0.96])
fig.savefig('dashboard_summary.png', dpi=200, bbox_inches='tight')
plt.show()

Course Summary¶

Data cleaning covered: missing values (dropna, fillna, forward/backward fill, interpolation), duplicate removal (exact and key-based), data type conversion (astype, pd.to_numeric, pd.to_datetime), text cleaning (str.strip, str.lower/upper/title, str.replace, str.contains, str.extract, str.split), categorical standardisation with mapping dictionaries and np.where, outlier handling (IQR method, domain-rule cleaning, clip), and column renaming and reordering.

Data manipulation covered: selection and filtering (loc, iloc, boolean indexing, isin, between, query), sorting (sort_values, nlargest, nsmallest), new columns (vectorised arithmetic, apply, lambda, np.select), groupby and aggregation (including named aggregation), pivot_table and crosstab, reshaping (melt, pivot, stack, unstack), merging and concatenation (merge with every join type, concat), binning (cut, qcut), ranking and cumulative statistics (rank, cumsum, diff, pct_change), time series tools (resample, rolling, the .dt accessor), MultiIndex operations, and apply / map.

Matplotlib charts covered: line, vertical bar, horizontal bar, stacked bar, grouped bar, histogram, box plot, scatter and bubble chart, pie chart, area chart, stacked area chart, step plot, stem plot, error bar plot, dual axis chart, multi-panel subplots, and saving a figure to file.

Seaborn charts covered: scatter plot, line plot, bar plot, count plot, box plot, violin plot, strip plot, swarm plot, histogram with KDE, KDE plot, ECDF plot, correlation heatmap, pivot-table heatmap, regression plot (regplot and lmplot), pair plot, joint plot, cat plot, point plot, facet grid, and theme / palette / context styling.
